summary: Defines the cid: and mid: URL schemes, which let one refer to messages and body parts of messages, such as an HTML part pointing to an image in the same multipart message.

plainLanguage.summary: Web-style links that point to a piece inside an email, like a picture attached to the same message.

questions: embed image in email with content-id
how to reference an image in an email body
subtitle: Two URL schemes, cid: and mid:, that let an HTML mail part point at an image or another message.

tldr.problem: Email that carries a Web page plus its images needs a way for the HTML to refer to the images inside the same message. News readers likewise need a way to refer to a message by its Message-ID.
tldr.mechanism: The cid: scheme wraps a Content-ID address and names one body part of a message. The mid: scheme wraps a Message-ID address, with an optional Content-ID after a slash, and names a whole message or a part of it.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2392 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 2111 and has not itself been obsoleted. It only refers to things, so it adds no new disclosure beyond the IDs it wraps.

today: RFC 2392 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 2111, and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it according to the unit metadata. The changes from RFC 2111 are corrected examples: a cid URL in the conversion example, Content-IDs with angle brackets and a Message-ID in the second example.

sections.title: Why Mail Needs Its Own URLs
sections.content:
MIME lets an email carry several pieces, called body parts (the RFC also calls them MIME entities). When mail conveys a Web page and its images, the HTML needs a URL scheme to refer to the image data that travels inside the same message. The cid: (Content-ID) scheme serves that purpose.

Net News readers have a related need: they use Message-IDs to link related messages together. The mid: (Message-ID) scheme gives them a way to refer to such a message as a resource.

RFC 1738 had already reserved the mid and cid schemes. This memo defines their syntax.
sections.plainLanguage: An email can hold a web page and its pictures in one package. These links let the page say which picture in the package it means, or which other message it is talking about.

sections.title: The cid: and mid: Syntax
sections.content:
Both schemes reuse the same building block, url-addr-spec, which is the URL encoding of an RFC 822 addr-spec. A cid URL is cid: followed by a content-id. A mid URL is mid: followed by a message-id, optionally followed by / and a content-id.

In a mail message the address in a Content-ID or Message-ID header sits inside angle brackets, but the URL leaves the brackets out. If the address contains a character that a URL does not allow, that character must be hex-encoded with the %hh escape from RFC 1738. This includes /, which is reserved inside the mid scheme.
sections.plainLanguage: A link is just the label of the thing you want, with any odd characters swapped for safe codes so the link does not get confused.

sections.title: Whole Messages, Body Parts and Uniqueness
sections.content:
A mid URL with only a message-id refers to an entire message. With the appended content-id it refers to a body part inside that message, as a cid URL does. The cid form is generally limited to references to other body parts in the same message as the referring part.

Both IDs are required to be globally unique: no two different messages share a Message-ID addr-spec and no different body parts share a Content-ID addr-spec. A technique the RFC mentions is to combine a time and date stamp with the local host's domain name, as in 950124.162336@XIson.com.

Content-IDs are unique, but many message stores do not index body parts apart from their message. The long mid form (message-id/content-id) was designed to supply that context.
sections.plainLanguage: Every message and every piece inside it has its own one-of-a-kind name tag. The long link gives both the envelope's tag and the piece's tag, so the mail program can find it even if it only files whole envelopes.

sections.title: What Implementations Must Do
sections.content:
A conforming implementation is required to support the long mid form. It may, but is not required to, use the uniqueness of Content-IDs to resolve a cid URL to any body part in the whole message store.

Sometimes one message holds several body parts with the same Content-ID, for example in multipart/alternate, where identical data can be reached through different methods. Conforming implementations are then required to follow the rules of the containing MIME entity to choose which part the Content-ID refers to.
sections.plainLanguage: Programs have to understand the long link. If two pieces share a name because they are different versions of the same thing, the program lets the package's own rules pick one.

sections.title: Converting Between URLs and Headers
sections.content:
To turn a cid URL into a Content-ID header, remove the cid: prefix, convert the percent-encoded characters back to US-ASCII, and put the rest between angle brackets. For example, cid:foo4%25foo1@bar.net corresponds to Content-ID: <foo4%25foo1@bar.net>. Reversing the steps and encoding URL special characters gives back the URL.

A mid URL converts to a Message-ID, or to a Message-ID and Content-ID pair, in a similar way.
sections.plainLanguage: To go from link to name tag, drop the starting word, undo the safe codes and add the little brackets. To go back, do it in reverse.

sections.title: The Two Examples
sections.content:
The first example is a message with a multipart/related container holding an HTML part and a GIF image part. The image part carries Content-ID: <foo4*foo1@bar.net>, and the HTML refers to it with an IMG tag whose source is a cid URL.

The second example is a message with its own Message-ID whose HTML contains a link to a different message. That link uses the long mid form, with a message-id, a slash and a content-id, and describes the target as 'hopefully still in the recipient's message store'.
sections.plainLanguage: In one example a web page inside an email shows a picture that is attached to the same email. In the other, an email links to an older email.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
These URLs only provide an addressing or referencing mechanism. They disclose no more about the originator's environment than the corresponding Message-ID and Content-ID values do.

Where disclosure is a concern, the originator of a message that uses mid and cid URLs must take precautions so confidential information is not revealed. The RFC notes that such precautions should already exist for ordinary use of Message-ID and Content-ID.
sections.plainLanguage: These links reveal nothing that the name tags did not already reveal. If a name tag gives away a secret, hide it in the first place.

data.title: cid and mid URL syntax
data.code:
content-id    = url-addr-spec
message-id    = url-addr-spec
url-addr-spec = addr-spec  ; URL encoding of RFC 822 addr-spec
cid-url       = "cid" ":" content-id
mid-url       = "mid" ":" message-id [ "/" content-id ]
